segment_name: The New Grub Street: Ambition, Poverty, and the Literary Marketplace

questions.question: Oliver, I want to start with you because you said something in our chat that I keep turning over — you called this a comedy. Not a tragedy, a comedy. And I think that's going to make Edmund's eyebrows go up. So make the case: in a novel full of hunger and humiliation and broken marriages, where's the comedy?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform his strongest take — the vaudeville/grotesque reading — and immediately bait Leigh into disagreeing about whether moral seriousness and comic observation can coexist

questions.question: Daniel, I want to put a specific moment to you — the scene where Reardon works out that to survive he has to write trash, that literary integrity has become something he literally can't afford. You said that's the novel's clearest exposure of a false choice. But Edmund is going to say that's Reardon making excuses — that the choice was always real, and Reardon blinked. Who's right?
questions.intent: Force the structural-vs-moral-character fault line into the open using a concrete passage; get Rosen and Leigh into direct disagreement about whether Reardon is a casualty or a coward

questions.question: Edmund, I have to put this to you directly: you said Gissing is a moralist and his verdict on Reardon is merciless — that he fails himself before he fails anything else. But doesn't that reading ask us to judge a man for not being a saint? What does Reardon actually have to work with here?
questions.intent: Push Leigh to defend his harshest claim and expose the tension between his moralism and the material conditions the novel depicts; invite Rosen and Trevelyan to pile in on the 'blame the victim' angle

questions.question: Let's talk about Jasper Milvain, because he's the figure everyone seems to have a different read on. Daniel, you said he's not the villain — he's the system made conscious and articulate, and that's actually more disturbing. Can you walk us through that? Because I suspect Oliver thinks Jasper is just the funniest character in the book, and Edmund thinks he's a moral warning. So who is this man?
questions.intent: Use Jasper as a lens to triangulate all three readings — comic grotesque, moral cautionary tale, systemic embodiment — and get all three experts responding to each other

questions.question: Oliver, I want to give you the last word on this before we open it up — you said Gissing finds the humor without betraying the pain. Can you find a moment in the text, a specific passage, where you can actually show us that working? Because I think that's either going to convince Edmund and Daniel or absolutely infuriate them, and either outcome is good radio.
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform a close reading of a specific passage that embodies his comic-yet-humane thesis; create a moment where the other two either convert or push back hard on the performance reading

steering_notes: The central fault line is Leigh vs Rosen — moral character vs structural determinism — and Trevelyan's comic reading cuts across both in a way that might either dissolve or intensify the disagreement. Keep pushing Leigh to specify what 'sufficient will' actually looks like in Reardon's material circumstances, because that's where his argument gets uncomfortable. Keep pushing Rosen on whether his structural reading leaves any room for individual agency at all — or whether that's the point. Let Trevelyan be the wild card: his instinct to entertain and perform might be the thing that unlocks the passages most vividly for listeners. If the conversation gets too abstract, redirect to the body — hunger, cheap clothing, the sound of bad pens — Trevelyan flagged these as acoustic and physical, and that's a good reset button.
cross_engagement_targets: Leigh's claim that Reardon 'chose' degradation directly contradicts Rosen's structural argument that the choice was always illusory — this is the segment's most productive collision and should be forced into the open early

Trevelyan's insistence that Gissing is an entertainer, not a sociologist, cuts against both Leigh's moralism and Rosen's political reading — he should be pushed to demonstrate this with a passage rather than just assert it

Rosen's reading of Jasper as 'the system made conscious' is almost the inverse of Leigh's reading of Jasper as moral warning — both can't be entirely right, and putting them in dialogue over a specific Jasper scene should produce real sparks
Leigh's phrase 'tragedy of human weakness masquerading as social realism' is a direct challenge to Rosen's entire framework — Rosen should be asked to respond to it explicitly

segment_name: The Machinery of Decline: Reardon's Spiral into Obscurity

questions.question: Edmund, you've argued that the real tragedy here is Reardon's spiritual poverty — not what the world does to him, but what he reveals about himself under pressure. Give me the passage where you think Gissing makes that case most nakedly. Where does Reardon actually see himself clearly?
questions.intent: Get Edmund to read a passage showing Reardon's self-awareness and complicity, establishing the character-driven reading that Daniel and Oliver can then push against

questions.question: Daniel, you heard Edmund — he's saying the marketplace is just the occasion that reveals what was always broken inside Reardon. But you've been pretty insistent that this is a *system* we're watching, not a soul. So whose reading does Gissing actually want us to have?
questions.intent: Force the system-vs-character disagreement into the open and get Daniel to challenge Edmund directly — ideally with the argument that sympathetic character readings serve a conservative function

questions.question: Oliver, here's what I want to put to you — both Daniel and Edmund are treating this as either a sociological document or a moral study, and you've said that misses the entertainer's coldness in Gissing's prose. So find me the moment where Reardon's humiliation tips into something almost farcical — where Gissing is clearly *enjoying* this. Where does the comedy live?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read the passage about accumulated humiliations or Amy confrontations and introduce the grotesque-comedy angle, which will genuinely unsettle both other experts

questions.question: Daniel, you said Reardon's most radical moment is his *refusal to grovel* — that when he doesn't internalize the shame, the machinery has to work harder. But Oliver's just shown us Gissing laughing at him. Can a man be both the novel's political conscience and its vaudeville turn? Does Gissing let him be both at once?
questions.intent: Create a three-way collision — Daniel's resistant Reardon vs Oliver's pathetic Reardon vs Edmund's self-deceived Reardon — and see if anyone can hold all three readings simultaneously

questions.question: Edmund, final push — Daniel says the novel's politics live in Reardon's resistance, Oliver says Gissing refuses to make us like him. Where does your moralist Gissing sit with that? Is there any version of Reardon that survives this book with his dignity intact, or is that precisely the point?
questions.intent: Give Edmund a closing synthesis moment that forces him to either defend his reading against the combined weight of the other two or concede interesting ground — either answer makes good radio

steering_notes: The productive fault line is system vs character vs aesthetic — keep pushing all three experts back to the text rather than letting this become abstract. Oliver is the wild card; his comedy reading will genuinely irritate Edmund and interests Daniel, so use it as a grenade when the system-vs-character debate goes circular. Don't let Edmund get too comfortable in the moral high ground — Daniel will want to argue that reading is itself ideologically convenient, and that tension is gold. The goal is to end the segment without resolving the disagreement: was Reardon destroyed, did he destroy himself, or did Gissing just use him for sport?
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund's claim that 'men of stronger character might endure' directly invites Daniel's counter that this is precisely the ideology Gissing is anatomising — the myth that poverty reflects interior weakness. Get them face to face on this.

Oliver's 'entertainer's coldness' reading cuts against both Daniel's political Gissing and Edmund's moralist Gissing — he should be pushed to say whether Gissing's ruthlessness makes the social critique *more* or *less* powerful, not absent.

Daniel and Oliver actually agree the novel is about the system rather than the man's soul, but disagree on tone — Daniel wants outrage, Oliver wants dark comedy. That's a productive near-agreement that Edmund can be used to destabilise.

segment_name: Comic Desperation: Humor and Survival in the Hack's Life

questions.question: Oliver, you've talked about Gissing having almost vaudeville timing — that the comedy lives in the *pacing*, the way a character's desperate optimism gets punctured by the very next paragraph. Can you actually show us what you mean? Pick a moment from the novel where that rhythm does its work.
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to read and perform a passage, establishing the stylistic argument early and grounding the conversation in the text before the ideological debate kicks off

questions.question: Daniel, you've said that when Reardon jokes about his poverty he's not being plucky — he's being 'murdered in slow motion.' But Oliver's just shown us Gissing clearly relishing the grotesque detail, almost enjoying himself. Isn't there a tension there? Can a novel be this *funny* about something and still be the radical indictment you're describing?
questions.intent: Force Rosen to either reconcile his systemic reading with Trevelyan's formal argument or double down on the idea that the comedy is itself a form of extraction — should produce a productive clash

questions.question: Edmund, you've described Gissing's compassion as essentially Christian-humanist — he mocks the folly but never the suffering, you said. But Daniel would say that framing lets the *system* off the hook entirely. When Jasper Milvain sharpens his pencils and philosophises about the new journalism, is that really a story about weak will meeting circumstance — or is Gissing showing us a man who's actually making the *rational* choice?
questions.intent: Draw out the direct Leigh-Rosen disagreement on whether character or capitalism is the novel's real subject, using the Jasper passage as the concrete battleground

questions.question: Edmund, you mentioned a passage you wanted to bring — Reardon's internal debate about accepting hack-work, where he tells himself it's only temporary. Oliver called that kind of moment 'the performance cracking.' Daniel would probably call it the system colonising consciousness. What do *you* call it — and does the comedy make it better or worse?
questions.intent: Get all three readings of the same type of moment on the table simultaneously, forcing the experts to triangulate against each other on Reardon specifically

questions.question: Last one — and I want everyone in on this. Daniel, you said that laughter under these conditions is just another form of unpaid labor the system extracts from the weak. Edmund thinks that's too cold — that Gissing's humor is the sign of genuine compassion. Oliver thinks the comedy is what *makes* you feel the tragedy rather than just understand it. Can all three of those things be true at once — or does one of them have to give?
questions.intent: Force a three-way synthesis or open disagreement as a closing move, letting each expert defend their strongest take while reacting to the others — good radio ending

steering_notes: Open with Trevelyan's formal argument and a passage reading to keep it grounded and listenable before the ideological debate opens up. The core tension to cultivate is Rosen versus Leigh — capitalism versus character — with Trevelyan as a useful third voice who keeps pulling both back to the text and the performance of the prose. Don't let the conversation stay abstract for more than two exchanges; push for specific passages. Watch for the moment where Leigh and Rosen's disagreement becomes genuinely heated — that's the segment's peak and worth slowing down for rather than mediating too quickly.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen's 'laughter as unpaid labor' claim directly contradicts Leigh's 'compassion that never mocks suffering' reading — these two framings are mutually exclusive and should be put in direct collision around the Reardon hack-work passage

Trevelyan's insistence that Gissing is an entertainer first cuts against both Rosen (who reads the comedy as symptom) and Leigh (who reads it as moral diagnosis) — worth making explicit that Trevelyan is actually disagreeing with both of them, not just one

Leigh's Jasper passage (the pencil-sharpening, the new journalism philosophising) is the same type of moment Rosen calls 'rational capitulation' and Trevelyan calls 'the performance of hope' — staging all three readings of that one passage would be the segment's most productive cross-engagement

segment_name: Milvain's Ascent: The Ruthless Logic of Literary Success

questions.question: Oliver, you've said Gissing actually loves Milvain — that there's real comic delight in watching him work. Can you find us a passage where you can actually hear that, where Gissing's prose is almost enjoying the con as it happens?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to read a passage showing Milvain's social manipulation as performance, and establish his 'comic masterpiece' reading before the others push back

questions.question: Edmund, you've called Milvain a man of 'weak character' — but Oliver's just shown us Gissing practically cheering him on. Is Gissing pulling us into admiring a cad, or is there something else going on? Where does the novel actually judge him?
questions.intent: Force Leigh to locate the moment of moral judgment in the text, and set up his 'cautionary figure' reading against Trevelyan's comic reading — productive friction

questions.question: Daniel, you've said condemning Milvain individually is exactly how we avoid the real indictment — that he's the system made flesh, not a bad apple. But Edmund's just pointed to Gissing showing us Milvain choosing, making small compromises. Doesn't Gissing need us to believe in individual choice for any of that to land?
questions.intent: Draw out Rosen's structural reading and put it in direct collision with Leigh's moral psychology argument — the sharpest disagreement in the room

questions.question: There's a passage you mentioned — Reardon's destruction running alongside Milvain's rise. Can you take us there? Because I want to hear whether the novel is actually making a structural argument in its form, or whether that's a reading we're imposing on it.
questions.intent: Get Rosen to read the juxtaposition passage and make his most radical claim — that the novel's structure enacts capitalist logic — which Leigh will want to challenge on literary grounds and Trevelyan on comic-aesthetic grounds

questions.question: Oliver, you said there's a moment after Milvain gets what he wants where the victory feels hollow — and you said Gissing's deflation is almost surgical there. Can we end on that passage? Because I want to ask all three of you: is that hollowness Gissing punishing him, or is it something more uncomfortable than that?
questions.intent: Close the segment with the most ambiguous, resonant moment — lets all three readings (comic tragedy, moral failure, structural indictment) compete for the same passage, and ends on an open question rather than a verdict

steering_notes: The key fault line is whether Milvain's rise is best understood as individual moral failure (Leigh), systemic inevitability (Rosen), or darkly comic performance (Trevelyan). Don't let this become abstract too fast — keep pulling back to specific passages and specific moments of choice. The most productive collisions will be Leigh vs Rosen on whether structures or character drives the tragedy, and Trevelyan vs Leigh on whether Gissing is judging or enjoying his creation. Watch for Rosen and Trevelyan finding unexpected common ground (both resist moralizing Milvain) — that could be a good moment to isolate Leigh and see if he holds his position. Let the final passage question breathe; don't rush to resolve it.
cross_engagement_targets: Trevelyan's 'Gissing loves Milvain' claim directly contradicts Leigh's 'cautionary figure' reading — push this collision early and let it run; they're both right in different registers and the tension is generative

Rosen and Trevelyan actually agree that moralizing Milvain misses the point, but for opposite reasons (Rosen: it obscures structural critique; Trevelyan: it obscures the comic genius) — surface this unexpected alliance and see if Leigh can dislodge either of them

Leigh's insistence that 'many in the same world remain decent' is the claim Rosen most wants to destroy — get Rosen to name who those decent characters are and what happens to them; Reardon is the obvious answer and it proves Rosen's point

The hollow-victory passage Trevelyan wants to read is also the passage Rosen would use for structural argument and Leigh for moral judgment — same text, three incompatible readings; that's the segment's climax

segment_name: Marian's Silence: Trapped Between Intellect and Circumstance

questions.question: Edmund, you said something in our chat that really stuck with me — that Marian isn't noble in her silence, she's *pitiable*, and that Gissing actually loves her for that. That's a pretty provocative claim. What do you mean? Because a lot of readers — myself included, honestly — come away from Marian's sections feeling like she's been dealt a genuinely rotten hand.
questions.intent: Get Edmund to lead with his strongest, most counterintuitive take — that Marian's fate is a moral failing not just a social one — which will immediately provoke both Oliver and Daniel

questions.question: Daniel, I can practically hear you bristling. Because your whole argument is that framing this as Marian's personal failure is itself doing the novel's ideological dirty work, right? Like — the system needs us to say she lacked courage, so we don't ask who profits from her silence. Can you make that case concretely — is there a specific moment in the text where you can show us the economic machinery operating on her?
questions.intent: Get Daniel to trace the economic argument through a specific passage — ideally the moment where Marian's education becomes a liability — and force the debate into the text rather than abstraction

questions.question: Oliver, you're in an interesting position here because you don't entirely agree with either of them. You told me you think Gissing actually writes Marian with a kind of dark comic awareness — that she *knows* how absurd her situation is. Where do you see that? Because if you're right, that changes everything — she's not pathetic and she's not purely a victim of the system. She's something stranger and more uncomfortable than either.
questions.intent: Draw out Oliver's formal argument about the gap between Marian's interior voice and her exterior performance — ideally getting him to quote a passage where another character misreads her silence as sweetness

questions.question: Edmund, can I push on something? Oliver's just argued that the reader *hears* Marian's thoughts while everyone around her stays deaf — that her silence is actually the most eloquent thing in the book, a formal trick Gissing pulls off brilliantly. But your reading implies that eloquence is wasted because she doesn't act on it. So here's my question: does Marian's self-awareness make her situation more tragic, or does it actually make her more culpable in your view?
questions.intent: Force the crux disagreement between Edmund and Oliver into the open — is Marian's inner life evidence of her dignity or evidence of her failure of nerve? Get Edmund to commit

questions.question: Last one — and I want all three of you on this. Daniel, you said Marian is *exemplary*, not exceptional — that she shows us what the system does to all women, just more visibly because she's smart enough to feel the trap closing. But here's the tension I keep coming back to: if Gissing's novel is as radical as you say, why has it taken so long for critics to read it that way? Is the book hiding its radicalism somehow — or have readers just been looking the other way?
questions.intent: Open a closing meta-question about the novel's reception and its political legibility — invites all three to weigh in on whether Gissing is radical, ambivalent, or co-opted by the ideology he's supposedly critiquing

steering_notes: The big fault line is Edmund vs Daniel — moral agency vs structural determinism — with Oliver cutting across both as the formalist wild card. Let Edmund establish his provocative take first so Daniel has something to push against, then use Oliver to complicate both positions before returning to Edmund for the crux question. Don't let this become an abstract debate about Marxism vs liberal humanism — whenever it drifts there, pull it back to the text. The gap between what Marian thinks and what she can say is the passage everyone should be fighting over. Watch for Edmund trying to cede too much ground to Daniel on economics while retreating to 'but it's still her choice' — that's the most interesting tension in his position. Also watch for Oliver and Daniel accidentally agreeing on the formal point (silence as indictment) while disagreeing completely on what it indicts.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund's claim that Marian 'chooses accommodation' directly contradicts Daniel's structural argument — the word 'choice' will be the flashpoint; push Daniel to respond the moment Edmund uses it

Oliver's reading of Marian's dark comic self-awareness sits uncomfortably between both positions — he agrees with Daniel that she's not morally culpable but agrees with Edmund that she has genuine interiority; get him to say explicitly which reading he's closer to

Daniel and Oliver both want to quote the gap between Marian's interior thoughts and her exterior performance — but they'll read that gap completely differently. Let them quote it and then ask Edmund to respond to the same passage with his reading

segment_name: The Narrative Game: Gissing's Technique and Moral Vision

questions.question: Oliver, you've said Gissing is one of the great comic novelists in English and we've basically forgotten how to read him that way. Make the case. Pick a moment — Jasper talking himself into something shabby, or one of those passages where the prose itself starts grinding like the work it's describing — and show us what we're missing when we read him as a gloomy social realist.
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform a close reading of a Jasper self-justification passage, establishing the 'comic performer' thesis as a provocation for Rosen and Leigh to push back against

questions.question: Edmund, you've called Gissing a novelist of the human soul, not a social novelist — and you're pretty firm about it. But Daniel would say that who gets a soul in this novel, whose inner life Gissing actually bothers to render, is itself a political choice. When Amy Reardon or a clerical worker recedes from the narrative and we're left swimming in Edwin's anxieties again — is that Gissing trusting our conscience, or is it Gissing just not being able to see certain people?
questions.intent: Force Leigh to defend his 'timeless human failing' reading against Rosen's structural critique, directly naming the interiority gap as a problem Leigh has to account for

questions.question: Daniel, you've argued that every time we're denied access to a poor character's mind, we're being trained in epistemic violence — that it's the whole point. But Oliver might say you're turning a comic novelist into a political theorist against his will. Is Gissing doing this *deliberately*, with full political consciousness? Or could the effect you're describing be real and devastating even if Gissing himself couldn't have told you that's what he was doing?
questions.intent: Push Rosen on the question of authorial intentionality vs. structural effect — opens a productive three-way on whether the 'political' reading requires Gissing to have meant it

questions.question: Oliver, there's a moment you mentioned — Biffen's quiet dignity, Edwin's exhaustion becoming almost unbearable. Those feel like a different register from the comic Jasper passages. When Gissing drops the satirical performance and just shows you someone losing without irony, does that complicate your reading? Is he still entertaining us there, or is something else going on?
questions.intent: Test the limits of Trevelyan's 'comic performer' thesis by pressing on the genuinely tragic passages — invites Leigh to claim those moments for his moral-soul reading and Rosen to argue they're where the class politics become undeniable

questions.question: Edmund, you've said Gissing blames the weakness of those who surrender — Reardon's failure is ultimately Reardon's. But Daniel and Oliver both seem to think the prose itself is doing something that undercuts that: either it's performing the seductiveness of compromise so well we feel it from the inside, or it's structurally refusing to let certain people even have a failure worth narrating. Can a novel that does those things really be asking us to just blame the individual?
questions.intent: Put the three readings into direct collision — Leigh's moral individualism vs. Rosen's structural critique vs. Trevelyan's performative complicity — and ask whether the technique actually supports the moral vision Leigh claims

steering_notes: The central tension is a genuine three-way: Leigh wants timeless moral drama, Rosen wants structural class critique, Trevelyan wants comic performance. The productive move is to keep showing how their readings aren't just different emphases but actually incompatible — especially on the question of whether the narrative gaps are intentional political choices (Rosen), morally generative silences (Leigh), or part of the satirical machinery (Trevelyan). Push for specific passages whenever things go abstract. The Biffen question is a good reset if the structural/intentionality debate gets too theoretical.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen vs. Leigh on interiority: Leigh claims the impersonal narrator makes us judge souls ourselves — Rosen says the choice of *whose* soul we get to judge is itself the ideological move Leigh won't acknowledge

Trevelyan vs. Rosen on intentionality: Trevelyan reads Gissing as a conscious performer; Rosen argues the structural effect is real whether or not Gissing 'meant' it politically — these are actually compatible but neither has spotted that yet, which makes it good radio

Leigh vs. Trevelyan on moral register: Leigh's 'novelist of the soul' thesis depends on Gissing being serious; Trevelyan's 'comic novelist' thesis complicates where the moral weight actually lives — get them to fight over the Biffen and Edwin passages specifically

All three on complicity: Trevelyan says the narrative makes us complicit in self-deception; Rosen says it makes us complicit in class blindness; Leigh says it makes us complicit in moral judgment. These are three genuinely different accounts of what reading this novel does to you.

segment_name: No Exit: Class, Talent, and the Impossible Choice

questions.question: Edmund, you've said that Reardon's real problem isn't the market—it's that he lacks what you called 'fibre.' That feels almost like a Victorian self-help lecture. But isn't Gissing specifically showing us a man who *can* see clearly, who *does* know what's happening to him, and still can't escape it? Where does moral will enter into that?
questions.intent: Get Edmund to defend his character-failure reading at its most exposed flank, opening the door for Daniel to pile in with the structural counter-argument and Oliver to argue that the whole point is complicity, not cowardice

questions.question: Daniel, I want to push you on Jasper Milvain—because Jasper isn't a victim, he's a winner. He's charming, self-aware, completely honest about what he's doing. Does his success prove your argument about the system, or does it actually complicate it? Because Edmund might say Jasper just has *more* of what Reardon lacks.
questions.intent: Force Daniel to reckon with Jasper as the system's chosen instrument, and bait Edmund into claiming Jasper as a moral exemplar—which Oliver can then puncture by pointing to Gissing's comic presentation of him

questions.question: Oliver, you've said the novel is funny—darkly, precisely funny. I want to test that. Can you find a moment in the text where Gissing is clearly making us laugh, and then tell me what the joke actually *is*, because I suspect the joke might be on the reader as much as the characters?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to quote one of the grotesque minor character passages and articulate his 'comedian of catastrophe' thesis in concrete terms—then see if Daniel thinks the comedy lets the system off the hook, or if Edmund thinks it trivializes genuine moral failure

questions.question: There's a moment—and Daniel, I think you wanted to go here—where a character realizes their talent simply doesn't matter. Not that they're not good enough, but that *good enough doesn't count*. Can you read that passage and tell me: is that Gissing the radical, or Gissing the realist who just happened to see something nobody wanted to say out loud?
questions.intent: Get Daniel to quote the passage where the system's indifference to merit is most nakedly shown, and open the question of whether Gissing is diagnosing or indicting—a distinction Edmund will want to contest

questions.question: Edmund, last one for you—and I want a genuine answer, not a Victorian one. Amy. Is she a villain, a realist, or is she actually the only character in the novel who understands the situation clearly and acts on it? Because I think there's a version of your argument where Amy is the *hero*.
questions.intent: Force Edmund to either defend Amy as a figure of clear-eyed moral agency—which will infuriate Daniel, who sees her as the market's instrument—or qualify his moralism in a way that brings him closer to Oliver's complicity reading

steering_notes: The core tension to keep alive is between Edmund's character-failure reading and Daniel's structural reading—they are genuinely incompatible and both experts know it. Oliver is the wild card who can puncture both by pointing to Gissing's comic register as the actual argument. Don't let Edmund retreat into Johnsonian abstraction—push him toward specific characters and specific moments. Don't let Daniel turn this into a lecture on Victorian political economy—keep him in the novel. If the conversation stalls, ask whether *any* character in the book makes a genuinely free choice, and let them fight over that. The Amy question at the end is designed to be destabilizing—it should reframe the whole conversation in the last ten minutes.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund's claim that Reardon 'grinds himself down' directly contradicts Daniel's insistence that the system is the grinder—this is the segment's central fight and should be surfaced early and returned to
Oliver's argument that complicity is the real trap is a potential bridge between Edmund and Daniel but will satisfy neither—use it to complicate both positions when one side is dominating

Daniel's reading of Jasper as the system's logic made flesh sits awkwardly against Edmund's implied admiration for Jasper's self-knowledge—if Edmund concedes any respect for Jasper, press him on whether that means the market *is* a meritocracy

Oliver's insistence that the comedy is where the real argument lives will likely frustrate both Edmund (who reads the novel as moral tragedy) and Daniel (who reads it as structural critique)—use that friction to ask whether the humor is a feature or a flaw

The question of Amy's agency cuts across all three readings: Edmund needs her to be morally culpable, Daniel needs her to be structurally determined, Oliver will want to note that Gissing writes her with comic precision and something close to sympathy—all three responses should be in tension
